basis: Ushojo maalo father matches Shina maalo and Kundal maal in the mahallaka old-person/kinship family. Its explicitly initial syllable stress is retained against Gilgit late mora and Kundal rising tone, without pretending these source notations are identical.

Brokskat šcar father-in-law agrees with the contracted śvaśura kinship set; the medial affricate and exact vowel realization need source phonological interpretation, so the link is provisional at the fine segmental level.
Brokskat pus fertilizer matches Shina paaṣ manure and the pāṁśu soil/dung family in both consonants and a specifically documented manure sense; no accent is marked.
Ushojo aapo few directly matches Shina aapo/apo and álpa, including lp simplification and a final o adjective ending. Initial syllable stress does not identify first versus second mora.
Brokskat paades fifteen retains p...d...š compound-numeral material matching páñcadaśa, with independently observed initial stress and loss of the nasal/affricate cluster to be modeled separately.

Ushojo aŋguuli finger preserves aṅguli's nasal-velar/li structure and accents the medial syllable. Quantity differs from the short old u headword and must be distinguished from the *aṅgūḍi alternative.

Brokskat guli finger belongs ultimately to the aṅguli family, but SchmidtKaul2008p248 explicitly calls it a loan from an unidentified Indo-Aryan language. Its initial stress is loan evidence, not an inherited loss of prefixal aṅ.

Brokskat nuori fingernail matches Shina nooro/nuuro and the nakhara claw/nail family, with a final i cell. Primary p258 confirms initial stress, while the stored uo versus source uu reading requires exact transcription review.
Ushojo nokh fingernail retains the kh of nakhá rather than the r derivative nakhara. This independent segmental distinction selects the simpler input family without consulting accent.

Ushojo aŋgar fire matches áṅgāra charcoal/fire in consonants and meaning and explicitly stresses the second syllable. It adds a syllable-level counterpart to the proposed attraction from old short initial accent to later long ā, while survey length is unmarked here.
Ushojo kaaṭe firewood agrees with kāṣṭha wood derivatives and a final e grammatical form, explicitly initial-stressed. Its ending and cluster history distinguish it from Palula unextended kaaṭ.
Ushojo mace fish matches mátsya with ts/y affrication and final e; the short initial stress is independently observed and can be compared with the old barytone once the final formation is identified.

Ushojo poš five and Brokskat's p...š numeral printed in SchmidtKaulp275 belong to páñca. The stored Brokskat pods spelling is suspect and must not be used for exact segmental analysis without correcting against the scan.

Brokskat puzo flea plausibly matches plúṣi/pluṣa derivatives through initial cluster reduction and a final o extension, with initial stress. The z correspondence needs comparative confirmation, so this is a provisional etymological link.

Brokskat moos flesh directly matches māṁsá-family Shinaic meat forms. The printed p258Brokskat cell is unaccented moos; the DB's moós is not accepted as a Brokskat mora reading and is corrected in the research source observation.
Ushojo aṇṭhi flour matches the ārta/āṭa flour family and Shina nasalized aṭi-type forms, with initial stress and an i ending. Nasalization and the exact suffix remain formation-level questions.

Ushojo pušuru flower shares the puš floral root with Shina pušu; final uru is a further formation. The database púṣya headword competes with puṣpa, so this link is a floral root-family comparison, not acceptance of that specific old accent.
Brokskat coor and Ushojo car four match catvāraḥ through the characteristic c/r numeral structure; modern vowel differences and absent tone marking remain explicit.

Brokskat cuudes and Ushojo cadaš fourteen retain the four-plus-ten compound structure and both have initial syllable stress. This directly contrasts with later-stressed teen numerals in the same sources, but quantity and analogical remodeling must be tested jointly.
Ushojo carmoŋgo fourth contains the four root plus a renewed ordinal suffix moŋgo; it belongs to the fourth ordinal comparison set but is not a segment-by-segment reflex of caturthá.

Ushojo lu'i fox matches the lōpi/lōi fox family after p loss; final stress differs from legacy Shina lṓi and requires the source's diphthong/hiatus and feminine-cell interpretation. The longer lōmaṭaka alternative is not independently required by this short form.
Ushojo mewa fruit is the same regional meva word as the Shina survey forms, with final syllable stress. This is a contact-word comparison and supplies no Sanskrit accent baseline.

Ushojo furalo full has the pur-/puray fill root plus an al result-adjective formation, comparable with pūrita/pūrilo derivatives. The extra l and initial f need formation history; exclude from strict direct-participle predictions until resolved.
Ushojo jaṭ fur agrees with Palula jhaaṭ animal hair and the jhaṇṭa/jhaṭa expressive hair family, with matching retroflex final and animal-hair sense.
Brokskat gi ghee matches the ghr̥ta family after cluster reduction and contraction; the short unaccented token cannot distinguish old or modern mora accent.

The Ushojo phwi girl token is the same form as phwi daughter, matching the putrī-type feminine family provisionally linked above; the pōta/phoi girl formation remains an independent alternative requiring paradigmatic evidence.
Ushojo de give is the imperative dā-family root, distinct in grammatical cell from the reduplicated present dádāti and from the perfective datta.

Brokskat byaas and Ushojo bo go match the vraj/brajj go family and its independently attested ba/bo western reflexes. Brokskat s is recurring citation morphology; the exact vowel development and suppletion remain open.

Ushojo ai and Brokskat aau she-goat match the feminine ajā-type goat family through intervocalic j loss, independently supported by the older Brokskat ā attestation. Unequal vowel sequences and feminine formation prevent simple mora coding.
Ushojo šo good matches Palula šoo and the śubha good family through b/h loss. The unmarked monosyllable supplies no tone reading.
Brokskat pooc̣o grandson is explicitly first-stressed in the printed p261table and matches pautra with tr affrication. The DB acute is treated as stress, not evidence of a Brokskat mora contrast.
Brokskat ẓas grapes matches Shina ẓac̣/jac̣ in the drākṣā grape family. The exact s/retroflex outcome and possible contact transmission require comparison, while no tone is marked.

Ushojo daṣ grape has the regional d-initial grape form compared with Kashmiri dac and Guresi daṣ in SchmidtKaul2008p246n21. This may be contact-mediated rather than directly inherited; retain the hypothesis without equating it to a regular dr-to-d Shinaic law.
Brokskat gaas grass matches ghāsá grass in consonants, long root and meaning; it is distinct from kákṣa grass despite the shared gloss. Contact borrowing remains possible and no tone is written.
Brokskat niilo green matches nī́la and other Shinaic blue/green adjectives. Its initial prominence is syllable stress in this source, so no Brokskat early-mora claim is made.

Ushojo pešege ground is a past verbal form with peṣ/pēṣ root vocalism and extra eg morphology, compared provisionally with pēṣayati rather than automatically assigned to a piṣṭa participle. Keep the old immediate formation unresolved.

Ushojo mumpali groundnut is a regional compound ultimately involving mung-bean plus fruit/pod material, not a direct simple mudga reflex. The modern groundnut referent and compound accent are kept separate from inherited root accent.
